questions.solution: The antiderivative of 3x^2 is found by applying the power rule, which states that the antiderivative of x^n is (x^(n+1))/(n+1). For 3x^2, n = 2, so the antiderivative is (3x^(2+1))/(2+1) = x^3. Adding the constant of integration C gives us x^3 + C.
questions.explanation: The power rule is used to find antiderivatives of polynomial functions.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be forgetting to add the constant of integration C, which is essential in finding a general antiderivative.

questions.stem: Find the antiderivative of g(t) = e^t.
questions.solution: The antiderivative of e^x is simply e^x itself, since the derivative of e^x is also e^x. Adding the constant of integration C gives us e^t + C.
questions.explanation: The exponential function has a simple antiderivative form.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be trying to apply logarithmic rules, which are not applicable here.

questions.solution: The antiderivative of z^n when n ≠ -1 is z^(n+1)/(n+1). For 5z^(-2), n = -2, so the antiderivative is 5z^((-2)+1)/((-2)+1) = -5/zt. Adding the constant of integration C gives us -5/zt + C.
questions.explanation: The power rule with a negative exponent can be used here.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be forgetting to adjust the exponent when applying the power rule.

questions.stem: Find the antiderivative of j(x) = sin(x).
questions.solution: The antiderivative of sin(x) is -cos(x), as the derivative of cos(x) is -sin(x). Adding the constant of integration C gives us -cos(x) + C.
questions.explanation: The sine function has a well-known antiderivative form when paired with cosine.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be forgetting to include the negative sign in front of cos(x).

questions.solution: The antiderivative of cos(ax) is (1/a)sin(ax), where a is a constant. For 2cos(3w), a = 3, so the antiderivative is (1/3)sin(3w). Adding the constant of integration C gives us 1/3sin(3w) + C.
questions.explanation: The cosine function with a coefficient and variable inside the argument requires adjusting the coefficient in the antiderivative formula.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be forgetting to divide by the coefficient outside the trigonometric function.

questions.stem: Find the antiderivative of m(p) = p^(1/2).
questions.solution: The antiderivative of p^n when n ≠ -1 is p^(n+1)/(n+1). For p^(1/2), n = 1/2, so the antiderivative is p^((1/2)+1)/((1/2)+1) = p^(3/2)/3/2 = p^(1/2)/2. Adding the constant of integration C gives us p^(1/2)/2 + C.
questions.explanation: The power rule with a fractional exponent can be used here.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be forgetting to simplify the fraction in the denominator after applying the power rule.

questions.solution: The antiderivative of e^(ax) is (1/a)e^(ax), where a is a constant. For 4e^(2q), a = 2, so the antiderivative is (1/2)e^(2q). Adding the constant of integration C gives us 1/2e^(2q) + C. To simplify, we can multiply by 1/2 to get 1/8e^(2q) + C.
questions.explanation: The exponential function with a coefficient inside requires adjusting the coefficient in the antiderivative formula.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be forgetting to divide by the coefficient outside the exponential function.
